section.title: Greeting from the Elder
section.sectionRationale: The opening of the letter sets its whole key. In three verses the elder names his readers, roots his affection in the truth, and pronounces a blessing that binds truth and love together. Everything that follows, the charge to love and the warning against deceivers, grows from this ground.
section.thesis: The elder loves the chosen lady and her children in the truth, a truth that abides in every believer forever, and he blesses them with grace, mercy, and peace that come from the Father and the Son and are known in truth and love.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the writer and his readers; the truth that binds them; the blessing of grace, mercy, and peace.

units.label: The elder to the chosen lady

verses.text: The elder, To the {{eklekte|chosen}} lady and her children, whom I love in the {{aletheia|truth}}, and not I alone, but also all who know the truth,
because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever:
{{charis|Grace}}, mercy, and peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, will be with us in truth and {{agape|love}}.

eklekte.gloss: Chosen, elect, selected by God. The lady is addressed as chosen, echoing how the whole church is called God's elect. Whether the phrase names a particular Christian woman and her family or a local congregation and its members, the word grounds the readers' identity not in their own standing but in God's gracious choosing.

aletheia.gloss: Truth, reality, what is genuine and trustworthy. The word rings through this short letter, and here it is the very atmosphere of the elder's love: he loves them in the truth. Truth in John is not only right doctrine but the reality of God revealed in Christ, embraced and lived. It is the shared ground on which all who know God stand together.

charis.gloss: Grace, undeserved favour, God's kindness freely given. It heads the apostolic blessing, followed by mercy and peace. Grace is the fountain: God's unearned goodness in Christ from which mercy toward the needy and peace with God and one another both flow.

agape.gloss: Love, self-giving devotion that seeks another's good. Paired here with truth as the setting in which grace, mercy, and peace are enjoyed. For John, truth and love are never rivals; the same God gives both, and His people are meant to hold them together.

basic.context: This is the greeting of a very short, personal letter. An older leader, who simply calls himself the elder, writes to a Christian woman and her children, or perhaps to a whole church pictured as a lady and her members. He tells them he loves them, and that his love is bound up with the truth they share. Then he prays a blessing over them.
basic.hermeneutics: A New Testament greeting is more than a polite hello; it announces the letter's themes. Here the twin notes of truth and love sound at once, and they will run through the whole letter. The blessing is a real prayer, not a formality, and it names where grace, mercy, and peace come from: the Father and His Son.
basic.originalLanguages: The readers are the chosen, eklekte, an echo of God choosing His people. The word truth, aletheia, appears again and again in these verses; it is the reality of God in Christ, shared by all who know Him. The blessing is grace, charis, then mercy and peace, all enjoyed in truth and love, agape.
basic.typology: There is no formal type here, but the pattern is rich: God the Father and Jesus Christ the Son are named together as the one source of blessing, an early and clear witness to who Jesus is. The truth that abides forever points to the permanence of what God has done in Christ.
basic.christ: Jesus Christ is named as the Son of the Father, the joint source, with the Father, of grace, mercy, and peace. To place the Son beside the Father as the giver of divine blessing is to confess His deity. He is the truth in which the elder loves, and love and truth meet in Him.
basic.god: God is the Father who chooses a people and pours out grace, mercy, and peace. He is not distant but gives Himself, and He gives truth and love together. What God joins, His people must not tear apart.
basic.crossReferences: 1 John opens with the same union of truth and love. 3 John, also from the elder, greets a friend loved in the truth. Paul's letters open with grace and peace from the Father and the Son, the same confession of who Jesus is.
basic.oneStory: The letter opens where the whole Bible story arrives: a people chosen by God, loved in the truth, blessed by the Father and the Son. Truth and love, so often split apart in the world, are here held together in Christ, and that union is the ground of everything the elder will go on to say.

context.literary:
The opening has the shape of an ordinary Greek letter, sender, recipient, greeting, but John bends every part of it. A Roman writer would name himself, name the reader, and write one word, chairein, 'greetings.' Here the sender is only a title, the recipient is a lady and her children, and the single word of greeting is replaced by a blessing of three gifts and two companions, grace, mercy and peace, in truth and love. Everything the letter will go on to say is already folded into these three verses.

Notice how the word truth runs through the sentence like a thread. It is the sphere of the elder's love in verse 1, the shared possession of all who know it, the reason for the love in verse 2, and the climate of the blessing in verse 3. The sentence is one long unbroken chain, 'whom I love in the truth, and not I alone, but also all who know the truth, because of the truth that abides in us.' The reader hardly gets a breath, and that is the point: truth is not one topic among several but the ground under every other word.

The two ends of the verse are matched. The letter begins with 'the elder' and 'the chosen lady' and ends in verse 13 with 'your elect sister', so that the whole letter is framed by election language and by family language, a household writing to a household. The little reversal in verse 3 is also worth seeing. Grace, mercy and peace come from the Father and the Son, and they are enjoyed 'in truth and love.' The gifts come down from God, and they are received in a setting that the readers must keep in good repair, truth and love together.
context.historical:
Ancient letters were short, practical and public in a way ours are not. A letter like this would be carried by a trusted traveller and read aloud to a gathered group. Greek letters of the day opened with the writer's name, but John gives only the title 'the elder,' presbyteros, a word that simply means an older man and that had come to name a recognised leader in a congregation. He uses the same bare title in 3 John 1. It assumes the readers know exactly which elder is writing, which fits an author of great and well known standing, and early church tradition from Irenaeus onward identifies him as the apostle John, settled in Ephesus in his old age. The usual dating is the last decades of the first century, though the letter itself gives no date.

The recipients are a house church or a family. In the first century believers met in homes, as in Romans 16:5, 1 Corinthians 16:19 and Colossians 4:15, so a 'lady' with 'children' could be a household that hosted a congregation, or the congregation itself. The question matters for the warning in verses 10 and 11, which is about whom to receive 'into your home.'

The language of the greeting also carried a quiet claim. The word for lady, kyria, is the feminine of kyrios, 'lord,' and in a world where Caesar was routinely called lord, a letter that places the Father and Jesus Christ at the head of the blessing was making a political as well as a spiritual statement. John is not looking for a fight with Rome here, though; his concern is with a quarrel inside the church, with teachers who have left the apostolic circle, and with how far a household should go in welcoming them.
context.canonical:
The greeting stands in a family of New Testament openings, and its differences are instructive. Paul's letters regularly open 'grace and peace,' as in Romans 1:7. Only in 1 Timothy 1:2 and 2 Timothy 1:2 does he add 'mercy,' in letters to a younger co-worker. John uses the triple form in a letter to a community, and then adds two settings, truth and love, that no Pauline salutation includes. Peter's opening in 1 Peter 1:1-2 also speaks of the 'elect' and of obedience to Jesus Christ, so the idea that a congregation is first of all a chosen people is a shared apostolic assumption, not a private quirk of John.

The echoes within John's own writing are close. The first letter opens with the same pair of themes. It speaks of eternal life 'which was with the Father and was revealed to us,' and of fellowship with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ, 1 John 1:2-3, which is exactly the double naming of verse 3 here. The Gospel's prologue describes the incarnate Word as 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14, and says that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. The opening of 2 John therefore compresses the Gospel's vocabulary into a greeting. Finally, 3 John 1 greets 'Gaius, whom I love in the truth,' using nearly the same phrase as verse 1, which is the strongest sign that the two short letters came from the same hand and were meant to be read together.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John writes to a community he loves and is worried about. He wants them to feel, before they read a single instruction, that the warning to come is a family matter and not an attack from a distance. That is why the letter does not begin with a rebuke. It begins with affection, with a reminder that others share his love and that it rests on something solid, and with a blessing that names God as its source.

He also wants the readers to see why truth and love matter at the very start. The people who are about to be called deceivers in verse 7 are, among other things, people who appeal to love without truth, or truth without love. By anchoring both in God and then in the readers' shared life, John makes it impossible to treat either as optional. The hearers are to understand that the God who gave them truth also gave them one another, and that to guard the first is to protect the second.

Finally he wants them to take heart. The truth that 'abides in us and will be with us forever' is a promise, not a burden, and the blessing assures the readers that God's grace, mercy and peace will be with them. In a season of confusion, when teachers were leaving and doubt was spreading, such confidence was exactly what a small church needed to hear before the hard words arrived.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The greeting describes a state of affairs, that the elder loves these people, that the truth abides in them and will, and it pronounces a blessing. It issues no command, and it would be a mistake to turn its description into one by reading, for example, that every Christian must send greetings in this exact form. What it describes is what the commands of verses 5 to 11 will protect.

The way to carry it forward is by example and by implication. If truth really does abide in believers and will be with them for ever, then holding fast to what the apostles taught is not a gritted-teeth duty but a response to something God has already put within them. And if the elder's love is rooted in truth, then affection that has no concern for doctrine, or doctrine held with no affection, both fall short of the pattern. The greeting also gives a model for how to begin hard conversations: with honest love, with confidence in what God has done, and with a prayer for the other person's good.

debates.question: Is the 'chosen lady' an individual or a church?

views.label: An individual Christian woman with her household
views.case: The letter reads like ordinary correspondence to a real person. The addressee is singular in verses 1, 5 and 13, a lady with biological children, and the elder rejoices over some of them in verse 4. Greek has no difficulty with a personal name or title at this point. The warning about whom to receive into 'your home' in verse 10 fits a woman who hosted a house church.

views.label: A local congregation addressed as a lady
views.case: Several details shift to the plural in verses 6, 8, 10 and 12, as though a community stands behind the singular. The city or church as a woman with children is an old biblical picture, as with Zion in Isaiah 54:1 and the bride in Revelation 21:2, and the church in Babylon is called 'chosen together with you' in 1 Peter 5:13. On this view the elect sister of verse 13 is a sister congregation.

debates.bearing: The shift between 'you' singular and plural makes certainty hard, and neither reading changes what the elder asks. In either case the readers are a gathered group of believers responsible for what happens under their roof, and the letter's counsel is the same.

debates.question: Is 'the elder' the apostle John?

views.label: The apostle John, writing from Ephesus
views.case: Second-century writers including Irenaeus ascribe the letters to John the disciple of the Lord, and the language, with its truth, love, abiding and 'from the beginning,' is so close to the Gospel and 1 John that common authorship is the simplest explanation. Peter calls himself a fellow elder in 1 Peter 5:1, so an apostle could use the title of humility.

views.label: A different leader, sometimes called John the elder
views.case: Eusebius preserves a report from Papias that speaks of an elder John in the circle of the apostles' disciples. Some argue that the bare title 'the elder' fits a figure with that name, distinct from the apostle, and that the letters come from his school.

debates.bearing: The letter's authority rests on its content and its fit with the apostolic message, and both views accept that. Even those who prefer another elder agree that he writes in the apostolic tradition of the Gospel, so the reader loses little by leaving the question open.

study.originalLanguages:
The title in verse 1, ho presbyteros, is a comparative form of the word for old, and by the time of the New Testament it names a recognised leader of a congregation, as in Acts 14:23 and Titus 1:5. John uses it with no name attached, which suggests the writer's identity was too well known to need spelling out. The same word in plural describes the leaders Paul summons from Ephesus in Acts 20:17.

The lady is kyria, the feminine of kyrios, 'lord.' Whether it could be a proper name is debated, but the word appears with a definite sense in verse 5, 'dear lady,' and the plural 'you' of verses 6, 8, 10 and 12 keeps the community in view. Greek handles the switch between singular and plural easily.

The verb 'abides' in verse 2 is menein, the verb of John's whole theology of remaining. It describes the truth dwelling within believers in the present, 'abides in us,' and the following clause carries it forward 'with us for ever.' The Gospel uses the same verb for the Spirit who remains with the disciples, John 14:17, and for the disciples remaining in Jesus, John 15:4. When 2 John 9 later speaks of 'remaining in the teaching,' the reader is meant to feel the weight of this word from verse 2.

The phrase 'all who know the truth' in verse 1 uses a perfect participle of ginosko. In Greek the perfect pictures a knowledge that was reached and still stands, not a passing impression. The hearers do not merely have opinions about the truth; they have come to know it and still do. John also avoids the word 'faith' here, and speaks of knowing, because for him to know the truth is to be in living contact with the Father and the Son, John 17:3.

In verse 3 the three gifts are grace, mercy, eleos, and peace. Eleos is the word the Septuagint regularly uses for the covenant faithfulness of God, chesed, so mercy here carries the sense of God's steady kindness to His own people. The verb that governs them, estai, 'will be,' is a future indicative and not a wish, so that John does not say 'may grace be with us' but states that it will be. The preposition 'from,' para, is repeated, 'from God the Father and from Jesus Christ,' giving each a place in the giving of the blessing, with the title 'the Son of the Father' tying them together in one phrase.

typology.type: The chosen household as the people of God
typology.fulfillment: Israel was addressed throughout the Old Testament as God's chosen people, Deuteronomy 7:6, and the exiles of 1 Peter 1:1-2 are called elect in the same breath as that old identity. John's chosen lady and her children are a smaller echo of the same pattern: a family, a household, a church marked out by God's choosing, not their own. In Christ the pattern widens beyond one nation to all who believe, and the people are no longer defined by descent but by truth and love. The type falls short in that earlier Israel was a mixed company, while the chosen people here are known by their confession of Christ.

typology.type: The blessing from the Father and the Son
typology.fulfillment: The priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 put God's grace, His face and His peace on the people of Israel through the lips of Aaron's line. The apostolic blessing of verse 3 passes the same gift through the apostolic word, but now names two givers, the Father and Jesus Christ the Son. What the priests could only ask of God, the letter announces as already given in Him who is the truth. The pattern breaks off at the point of mediation: the old blessing needed priests, while this one flows straight from the risen Son who is Himself our high priest, Hebrews 4:14.

Isaiah 40:8 says that the word of our God stands for ever, while the grass withers. John says the truth abides in believers and will be with them for ever, which suggests that the same enduring word has become a settled possession of the people of God. The fulfilment is in Christ, who said that His words would not pass away, Matthew 24:35, and who is the truth, John 14:6. The correspondence is a promise of permanence, and it stops short of saying that believers are untroubled; the very letter that promises permanence warns that deceivers are abroad, and so the truth is kept by being held.

study.christ:
The greeting leads to Christ by confession. The blessing of verse 3 names two sources, the Father and Jesus Christ, and then calls the second 'the Son of the Father,' a title that appears nowhere else in the New Testament in this exact form. In a letter whose main business is a warning against those who deny the true identity of Jesus, this is no accident. Before John says a word against the false teachers, he plants a positive confession: Jesus is the Son who stands with the Father as the giver of grace, mercy and peace. Only God can give these gifts, and Jesus gives them along with the Father.

It leads to Christ by the word truth. In the Gospel Jesus does not merely speak the truth; He says, 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6. John's own prologue declares that the Word became flesh and was 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14, and that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, John 1:17. The grace and truth of verse 3 and the 'truth that abides in us' of verse 2 are therefore not abstractions. They are what believers have in Him. To say that the truth abides in us is, in John's thinking, to say that Christ abides in us, since the truth is a person before it is a body of ideas. The prayer of Jesus makes the same link when He says to the Father, 'Your word is truth,' John 17:17.

It leads to Christ by love. The elder's love for the readers is 'in the truth,' and verse 5 will tell them to love one another as the command from the beginning. For John, this love has a face. 'As I have loved you, so you also must love one another,' John 13:34. The love in verse 3 flows from the same Son who loved His own to the end.

It is worth noting the restraint. The greeting does not argue for the deity of Christ; it assumes it and lets the blessing's structure speak. The confession is quiet and settled, which is exactly the ground on which the letter will later stand when it challenges the teachers who have left the apostolic message. The reader meets Christ here not as a topic of debate but as the One in whom truth and love are already joined and from whom blessing is already coming.
study.god:
The greeting shows God first as the source of everything the church has. Grace, mercy and peace come from God the Father, and the Father is named before any human relationship is mentioned. The community does not manufacture its own unity; it receives it. The same grace by which they were chosen, verse 1, is the grace that now blesses them, verse 3, so the God of election and the God of ongoing blessing are one.

He is a God of truth in a way that shapes everything. John says that the truth abides in believers and will be with them for ever, which means that the truth is not a fragile deposit left unguarded. God Himself keeps it with His people. At the same time the letter will go on to say that this truth can be abandoned by those who do not remain in it, verse 9. Both statements are held together: God's faithfulness is certain, and human responsibility is real. The same tension runs through the Gospel, where the Father keeps the sheep and yet the sheep are told to remain.

He is a God of love who does not let love float free of truth. The greeting names both, side by side, and refuses to rank one above the other. What the world often splits, a warm heart with no convictions on one side and cold correctness on the other, God binds up in Himself. His own character is the model, since the Father is the God of truth, Psalm 31:5, and also the God who is love, 1 John 4:8.

He is a Father who has a Son. The first thing the letter says about God's identity is relational: Father and Son. The God of the Bible is not a solitary being who happens to have created, but a Father who loves a Son and gives Him as the way of blessing, John 3:16. This shapes how believers worship. They do not approach a distant ruler, but come to the Father through the Son, and the greeting already points toward the claim of verse 9 that to have one is to have the other.

For worship, the greeting teaches the church to receive before it acts. Before the elder asks anything of his readers, he reminds them of what God has already given, and that order is the shape of the whole Christian life: gift first, then obedience, grace first, then walking in love.

crossReferences.note: The first letter opens with the same pair of concerns, fellowship with the Father and with His Son, and with the aim that joy may be complete. Reading the two openings side by side shows that 2 John is a compressed companion to 1 John, and that the elder's confidence in the apostolic message begins at the very first line.

The elder's greeting to Gaius, whom he loves in the truth, is almost the same as verse 1 here. The echo is the clearest sign that the two short letters come from one hand and belong together, one to a lady and her children and one to a beloved friend.

The Gospel prologue says the incarnate Word was full of grace and truth, and that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. The grace and truth in verses 2 and 3 are the same gifts, now spoken of as the possession and the blessing of the church.

Jesus promises the Spirit of truth, who will be with the disciples and in them. This stands behind the claim that the truth abides in believers and will be with them for ever, and it shows that the abiding of verse 2 is the work of God's own presence in His people.

Paul's greeting to Timothy uses the same triple form, grace, mercy and peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. The shared form shows that John and Paul worked from a common apostolic pattern of blessing that put the Father and the Son side by side.

Peter addresses believers as the elect, chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit. His opening explains the confidence behind the title 'chosen' in verse 1 and shows the same apostolic habit of grounding the church's identity in God's choice.

Peter's closing sends greetings from the church in Babylon, 'chosen together with you.' It is a close parallel to the elect sister of verse 13 and supports reading the elect lady and her sister as communities rather than only individuals.

Paul sends greetings to the church in the house of Nympha. The verse shows how ordinary it was for a congregation to be identified with one household, and so helps explain how a lady and her children could be the readers of a letter addressed to a church.

The priestly blessing asks that the LORD bless His people, make His face shine on them, be gracious to them and give them peace. It is the Old Testament root of the apostolic blessing, now spoken in the name of the Father and the Son.

Jesus prays that the Father will set His people apart in the truth, and says that the Father's word is truth. This explains why truth is so central to the elder's love, since the truth is God's own word that sanctifies the church.

study.oneStory:
Scripture begins with a God who speaks truth and creates a world where that word is reliable. The first break in the story, in Genesis 3, is a break in trust: the serpent contradicts what God has said. From that moment the Bible's story is partly a story of truth being lost and found, of people building on lies and God sending His word again. The elder's greeting belongs near the end of that story, where the true word has been spoken in full by the Son, John 1:14, and a people have been gathered who know it.

The chosen lady and her children also belong to a long line of family language in the Bible. God called Abraham and promised a household that would become a nation, Genesis 12:2, redeemed that household from Egypt as His firstborn, Exodus 4:22, and finally made a new family of those born of God, John 1:12-13. The letter's small circle of believers is a living piece of that promise: chosen not for their own sake but as part of the people God is gathering.

The blessing of verse 3 is also a point where the story's two halves meet. Grace and truth were once the very qualities by which God revealed Himself to Moses, Exodus 34:6, where He proclaims Himself abounding in love and faithfulness. In Christ those qualities become flesh and are given to the church. What Moses glimpsed, the church now has, and the letter greets its readers as those who live inside that revelation.

The story is not finished. The elder is writing in the middle of a conflict in which deceivers are still on the move, and his promise that the truth 'will be with us forever' looks ahead to a day when no deception remains. In the new creation the dwelling of God will be with man, Revelation 21:3, and the truth that is now guarded will be seen without any shadow. Until then, the church lives in the tension of the greeting, already chosen, already blessed, already in the truth, and still called to hold on to it together in love.

sermon.title: Truth and Love
sermon.why: Begg preaches directly on the opening of 2 John, 1:1-3, showing how the elder binds his love for the readers to the truth they share and how the letter's blessing joins truth and love in the Father and the Son. A clear, orthodox handling of this greeting.

quiz.q: How does the elder describe his love for the readers?

options.text: He loves them in the truth, together with all who know the truth.
options.note: Verse 1 grounds his love in the shared truth, joined by all who know it.

options.text: He loves them because they are his own family by birth.
options.note: There is real affection, but the text roots the love in truth, not natural kinship.

options.text: He loves them only for their usefulness to his ministry.
options.note: Nothing in the greeting reduces his love to usefulness.

options.text: He says he cannot really love people he has not met.
options.note: The opposite is true; all who know the truth share this love.

quiz.q: Where do grace, mercy, and peace come from in verse 3?

options.text: From God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father.
options.note: Verse 3 names the Father and the Son together as the one source.

options.text: From the Father alone, with the Son only mentioned in passing.
options.note: The Son is named as a joint source, not merely mentioned; both give the blessing.

options.text: From the elder's own authority as a leader.
options.note: The elder pronounces the blessing, but its source is God, not himself.
Grace and mercy are by definition unearned, given by God.

quiz.q: What two things does the greeting hold together?

options.text: Truth and love, named as the setting for God's blessing.
options.note: The letter's twin themes sound together from the first verses.

options.text: Truth and law, as rival demands on the reader.
options.note: Truth is central, but the pairing here is truth and love, not law, and they are not rivals.

options.text: Wealth and status, as marks of God's favour.
options.note: The greeting says nothing of wealth or status.

options.text: Fear and judgment, as the tone of the letter.
options.note: The tone is warm blessing; truth and love, not fear, frame it.

quiz.q: What does calling the readers chosen, eklekte, emphasise?

options.text: Their identity rests on God's gracious choosing, not their own merit.
options.note: The word points to God's electing grace as the ground of who they are.

options.text: That they had earned a special rank among believers.
options.note: It is about God choosing, not a rank they earned.

options.text: That only a tiny elite can belong to God.
options.note: The word describes God's people, not a narrow elite; the whole church is called elect.

options.text: That their standing depends on their family name.
options.note: Their standing rests on God's choice, not lineage.

questions: The elder loves his readers in the truth. How does sharing the truth about Jesus deepen your love for other believers, even those you have never met?
The truth abides in us and will be with us forever. What comfort is there for you in knowing that God's truth is a permanent gift, not something you must keep hold of by your own strength?
Grace, mercy, and peace come from the Father and the Son together. How does it shape your prayers to know these gifts flow from God and not from your own performance?
Truth and love are held together from the very first lines. Where are you tempted to choose one at the expense of the other, and what would it look like to hold both as this letter does?

translationNotes.note: The elder, presbyteros, likely designates the apostle John by his role and age rather than a mere office.
The chosen lady, eklekte kyria, can be read as a specific believing woman or as a figure for a local church; the Greek allows both, and the letter's application holds either way.
Some manuscripts read 'the Lord Jesus Christ'; the BSB follows the reading 'Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father', which underscores His relation to the Father as joint source of the blessing.
